What You Will Learn in This Chapter
Basic Array Traversal is the foundation of almost every coding interview problem.
Even advanced patterns like sliding window, prefix sum, greedy, DP, graph traversal,
and monotonic stack all depend on one basic skill:
Move through the input carefully, maintain the right state, and update the answer at
the right time.
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to solve problems where you need to:

Scan an array once

Track a maximum or minimum

Count elements

Maintain a running sum

Track the best answer so far

Compare neighboring elements

Modify an array in-place

Use a read/write pointer

Traverse from right to left

Build a result array

Handle negative numbers, zeroes, duplicates, and overflow

Explain O(n) time and O(1) space clearly

Recognize when simple traversal is enough

Recognize when another pattern is needed
This chapter may look easy, but do not underestimate it. Many medium problems are
just advanced forms of:

What is the current element?

Core Intuition
Maintain three regions:

[0 ... low-1]
= 0s
[low ... mid-1]
= 1s
[mid ... high]
= unknown
[high+1 ... n-1]
= 2s
Process nums[mid].

If 0: swap with low, move both low and mid

If 1: move mid

If 2: swap with high, move high only
21.4 C++ Code
class Solution {
public:
void sortColors(vector<int>& nums) {
int low = 0;
int mid = 0;
int high = nums.size() - 1;
while (mid <= high) {
if (nums[mid] == 0) {
swap(nums[low], nums[mid]);
low++;
mid++;
} else if (nums[mid] == 1) {
mid++;
} else {
swap(nums[mid], nums[high]);
high--;
}
}
}
};

22.6 C++ Code

class Solution {
public:
int trap(vector<int>& height) {
int left = 0;
int right = height.size() - 1;
int leftMax = 0;
int rightMax = 0;
int water = 0;
while (left < right) {
if (height[left] < height[right]) {
leftMax = max(leftMax, height[left]);
water += leftMax - height[left];
left++;
} else {
rightMax = max(rightMax, height[right]);
water += rightMax - height[right];
right--;
}
}
return water;
}
};

class Solution {
public:
bool check(string& s, int left, int right) {
while (left < right) {
if (s[left] != s[right]) {
return false;
}
left++;
right--;
}
return true;
}
bool validPalindrome(string s) {
int left = 0;
int right = s.size() - 1;
while (left < right) {
if (s[left] != s[right]) {
return check(s, left + 1, right) ||
check(s, left, right - 1);
}
left++;
right--;
}
return true;
}
};

30.1 Sliding Window Maximum
I use a deque of indices, maintaining values in decreasing order. The front is always
the maximum of the current window. Before adding a new index, I remove expired

This is symmetric to maximum. I maintain an increasing deque, so the front always
stores the minimum of the current window.
30.3 Max-Min Constraint Window
I maintain two deques: one decreasing for maximum and one increasing for
minimum. The current window is valid when max minus min is at most the limit. If
invalid, I move the left pointer and remove expired indices.

candidate start indices with increasing prefix sums. Smaller prefix sums are better

those candidate indices in a decreasing deque. This makes each transition O(1)

Given array nums, pick random index among indices holding maximum value.

int pickRandomMaxIndex(vector<int>& nums) {
int best = INT_MIN;
int count = 0;
int answer = -1;

if (nums[i] > best) {
best = nums[i];
count = 1;
answer = i;
